chunks: Rule of thumb for real square wave bandwidth. The question: What is the rule of thumb for the highest frequency content of a real square wave?
The rule is: bandwidth is about 0. 35 divided by the rise time. Rise time is how long an edge takes to climb.
Bandwidth is the highest frequency a circuit, cable or oscilloscope can pass without weakening it much. The rule tells you how fast your equipment must be to carry an edge.
Picture a thermometer dropped from a cold room into a hot one. The reading does not jump. It climbs over a few seconds.
A faster-responding thermometer climbs sooner, and it can also follow quicker temperature wiggles. Response speed and rise time are two views of the same sluggishness.
The rule puts a number on that link.
All three lines have slope -1 on log-log axes: halve the rise time, double the bandwidth.
The red line shows what a scope needs to be accurate: about four times the minimum to just pass the edge.
Rise time: time for a signal to go from 10% to 90% of its final value.
Bandwidth: the highest frequency a system passes at close to full strength (before it falls to about 70%, called the -3 decibels point).
Oscilloscope: an instrument that draws a voltage against time so you can see edges. Rule of thumb: a quick estimate, good enough for sizing.
Highest significant frequency: the top of the range that matters for a given edge ("Highest frequency in real vs ideal square wave").
A signal has a 1 nanoseconds rise time. The bandwidth needed is 0. 35 / 1 nanoseconds = 350 megahertz. An edge that is 10 times faster, 100 picoseconds, needs 10 times more: 3.
5 gigahertz. Now pick a scope to look at that 1 nanoseconds edge. A scope rated at exactly 350 megahertz would slow the edge it shows.
A common practice is to choose a scope several times faster, roughly 1. 5 gigahertz, so it changes the measured edge by only a few percent.
That is the whole idea: faster edge, more bandwidth, and the product stays near 0. 35.
"The rule is bandwidth equals 0. 35 over the 10 to 90 percent rise time. It comes from a single-pole RC: rise time is 2.
2 RC, and the 3 decibels bandwidth is one over 2 pi RC, so the product is 0. 35. A 1 nanoseconds edge needs about 350 megahertz. For spectral content the knee is often taken as 0.
5 over the rise time. I use it to size scopes, probes and filters, and to see that the edge, not the clock rate, sets the bandwidth."
